children: , the obesity-and-diabetes medicine leader, faced a fresh competitive data point Monday after Novo Nordisk

said CagriSema beat tirzepatide's 5-milligram dose in a late-stage diabetes study. Lilly shares still climbed about 1.2% to $1,166.74, suggesting investors were not treating the result as a decisive threat to the company's obesity franchise.

Patients taking CagriSema lost an estimated 12.4% of their body weight versus 9.1% for patients receiving the Lilly comparator, while Novo also reported non-inferior blood-sugar reduction. But the comparison comes with an important catch: the trial tested people with diabetes and used tirzepatide at 5 milligrams rather than its higher approved doses. That makes the headline percentage gap less straightforward than it first appears.

The valuation picture also adds context. The chart shows Lilly trading 24.8% below its GF Value estimate, with the stock at $1,166.735 versus a GF Value of roughly $1,550. CagriSema previously lost to Zepbound in an obesity-focused head-to-head trial, so dosage, patient population and eventual real-world adoption matter more than a single low-dose comparison. Novo expects an FDA weight-management decision in the fourth quarter, which keeps competitive pressure alive, but Lilly's bigger test will be whether CagriSema can translate approval into meaningful pricing power and market share.

title: Lilly Gains as Novo Wins a Lower-Dose Weight-Loss Round
